The case began in 2015, when Ørsted
approached the two tax authorities to avoid double taxation of the ​projects; after the authorities did not reach an agreement, they ​referred the matter to the advisory commission.
Danish authorities claimed 6.6B Danish ​crowns (~$1B) in taxes and interest related to the projects, which Ørsted
challenged, saying British subsidiaries developed, owned, and operated the projects and had already paid U.K. tax.
The commission found the projects had a "genuine legal and economic purpose" and were "primarily taxable" in the country where ​they are located ​and generate revenue, the company said.
